questions.question: So, how did you get here?
questions.lead: I've loved computers for as long as I can remember.
questions.answer: Technology had my attention long before it became my job. My career took a less obvious route: I started in aviation, found my way into UX, and eventually into frontend engineering. Looking back, each chapter taught me something I still use.

questions.question: What did aviation have to do with UX?
questions.answer: Aviation was my first professional world, and it made me pay attention to how people make decisions when clarity matters. UX gave me a new way to think about the same thing. Who is using this? What do they need to know? What happens when things don't go to plan?

scene.caption: Three questions before the first pixel

questions.question: When did you start building things?
questions.lead: When I wanted to make the whole idea real.
questions.answer: I liked designing interfaces, but I kept wanting to know what happened behind them. Learning frontend meant I could take something from a rough idea to a working interaction. Even the loading states, the empty screens, and the awkward little edge cases became part of the design.

scene.caption: A screen has more than one state

questions.question: What's your work at F24 like?
questions.lead: I work on software people need to be able to trust.
questions.answer: For four years I've helped build crisis management and critical communication software at F24. I built the original frontend in Svelte and now deliver work in React. It has taught me to think carefully about what a person sees when the situation is already stressful.

scene.caption: An illustrative moment in a critical workflow

questions.question: What details matter most to you?
questions.lead: Usually the ones no one notices when they work.
questions.answer: A failed refresh shouldn't wipe out the information someone already has. An older response shouldn't overwrite a newer one. Closing a panel should bring keyboard focus back to the right place. They're small decisions, but they say a lot about how much you care for the person using the product.

questions.question: And when you're building for yourself?
questions.lead: I follow the ideas I can't quite leave alone.
questions.answer: Second Voice explores rewriting while keeping the original words and changes visible. Flow turns something you say into a useful, editable action. Leu and Needle let me explore reading, learning and finding things differently. I love that personal projects give me room to be curious, try things, and own every detail.

scene.caption: Two ideas I wanted to make real

questions.question: What still makes you curious?
questions.lead: Those little 'wait, how does that work?' moments.
questions.answer: I love understanding the invisible parts of technology, whether that's DNS, TLS or what actually happens when you open a website. The part I enjoy most is turning a complicated idea into something another person can understand without feeling talked down to.

scene.caption: A single web request, made visible

questions.question: What kind of work makes you proud?
questions.lead: Work that's thoughtful, even where nobody's looking.
questions.answer: An interface should feel good, but it should also be accessible, resilient and honest about what's happening. I care about readable code, typed boundaries, proper tests and the next person who has to maintain what I've built. For me, good engineering is another way of looking after people.

scene.caption: A small example of care in the code

ending.label: One last thing
ending.question: It's nice to meet you.
ending.answer: I like working with people who notice the little things, ask good questions and care about how the finished product feels to the person using it. If that sounds like you, I'd love to hear what you're making.

shortVersion.title: Hi, I'm Miguel.
shortVersion.intro: Computers have fascinated me since I was a kid. The funny thing is, I didn't go straight into tech.
shortVersion.aside: I'm still that curious kid. I just get to build things now.

chapters.title: Aviation
chapters.text: That's where my working life started. It gave me a lasting respect for clear information, good decisions and the people relying on both.

chapters.title: UX design
chapters.text: I became interested in what makes a product feel understandable to a real person, not just look good in a mockup.

chapters.title: Frontend engineering
chapters.text: Now I get to bring both sides together, designing and building products people can actually use.

shortVersion.outro: These days I'm based in Berlin, working on critical communication software and making my own little experiments whenever an idea won't leave me alone.
shortVersion.copyText:
Hi, I'm Miguel Almeida.

I've loved computers since I was a kid. My career began in aviation, moved through UX design and led me to frontend engineering.

I'm based in Berlin and have spent four years building critical communication software at F24, first in Svelte and now in React. I also build my own products, including Second Voice, Flow, Leu and Needle.

I care about thoughtful design, reliable interfaces and making complicated things easier to understand.

miguelalmeida1592@gmail.com

editorial.title: I took the scenic route to code.
editorial.intro: I was the kid who loved computers. Getting here took a few unexpected turns through aviation and UX, and I'm glad it did. Here are eight little stories about what I learned along the way and what I love making now.
